source: QP01 Economic Trend (AQR: Brooks, Feilbogen, Ooi, Akant, April 2023)

reasoning_map.question: Can an investor earn trend-following-like returns by positioning each equity, bond, rate, currency and commodity market on trends in macro fundamentals (growth, inflation, trade, monetary policy, risk aversion) instead of past prices, and does this diversify stocks, bonds and price trend, especially in drawdowns? It matters because trend-following is held mainly as drawdown protection and price trend alone fails in sharp reversals.

thesis.statement: Because markets underreact to economic news, trading 12-month trends in five macro themes with theory-fixed signs earned a Sharpe ratio of about 1.1 (1970-2022, gross) with near-zero stock/bond correlation and gains in their worst drawdowns; capturing the same underreaction through different inputs, it is only moderately correlated with price trend (0.4), so a 50/50 blend (Sharpe 1.5) beats either alone in return and drawdown protection.

foundations.premise: Asset prices systematically underreact to new information, so news is incorporated gradually and creates trends.
foundations.support: citations: time series momentum evidence over 120+ years and single-stock underreaction studies; extended to index and bond markets by two studies

foundations.premise: Underreaction has behavioural causes (biased belief updating, herding, extrapolation, disposition effect).
foundations.support: citations to theory papers (Barberis-Shleifer-Vishny, Daniel-Hirshleifer-Subrahmanyam, Hong-Stein, Frazzini); not tested here

foundations.premise: For macro assets, the relevant news is mostly news about economic fundamentals, so price trends are only an indirect and sometimes misleading proxy for it.
Each theme has a stable, 'other things equal' sign of effect on each asset class (e.g. rising growth good for equities, rising inflation bad for bonds and good for the currency).
foundations.support: economic channels with citations (cash flows, Balassa-Samuelson, Katz-Lustig, Clarida-Waldman, Bernanke-Kuttner, Eichenbaum-Evans, Campbell); said to be 'empirically verified' contemporaneously but no test is shown

foundations.premise: If news has a persistent impact, the predictive sign of a news trend must equal its contemporaneous sign, so imposing that restriction limits data mining.
Twelve-month changes in consensus forecasts (or, before 1991, realized data lagged one quarter, equivalent under a random walk) measure the news investors receive.
foundations.support: assertion; random-walk equivalence stated, not tested

foundations.premise: Large stock and bond drawdowns rarely come out of the blue; they are usually preceded by deteriorating fundamentals (growth, hawkish policy).
Prices can stay disconnected from fundamentals for prolonged periods (bubbles), and later re-couple.
Investors value trend-following mainly for positive returns in market drawdowns.
Simple, long-history measures are less exposed to data mining, and a simple backtest understates what a richer real-time signal set could achieve.

mechanism_chain.to: gradual price adjustment, i.e. price trends
mechanism_chain.why: investors underreact to news (behavioural reasons cited), so prices incorporate it slowly

mechanism_chain.to: trailing trends in fundamentals predict subsequent returns, with the same sign as their contemporaneous effect
mechanism_chain.why: if news impact is persistent, part of it is still to come, so trading the news trend directly captures it without using price as a proxy

mechanism_chain.from: 12-month changes in five theme measures per country (consumption-weighted for commodities)
mechanism_chain.to: a long or short view in each equity, bond, rate, currency and commodity market
mechanism_chain.why: structural sign map per theme and asset class, motivated by economic channels

mechanism_chain.from: many modestly profitable views across lowly correlated themes and asset classes
mechanism_chain.why: theme and asset class composites have average pairwise correlation 0.06-0.07, so equal-risk diversification lifts the Sharpe ratio

mechanism_chain.from: deteriorating fundamentals before major stock or bond drawdowns
mechanism_chain.to: short positions already in place, so the strategy gains in those drawdowns
mechanism_chain.why: drawdowns tend to be precipitated by falling growth expectations or hawkish policy, which the growth and monetary themes register

mechanism_chain.from: same underreaction mechanism, different inputs (fundamentals vs prices)
mechanism_chain.to: positive but moderate correlation between economic and price trend
mechanism_chain.why: good fundamental news is followed by positive returns on average, so the two often agree, but not always

mechanism_chain.from: price trend wins in persistent moves and bubbles; economic trend wins in catalyst-driven reversals
mechanism_chain.to: the two draw down at different times
mechanism_chain.why: price trend loses at reversals almost by construction; economic trend loses when prices decouple from fundamentals

mechanism_chain.from: moderate correlation plus complementary drawdown coverage
mechanism_chain.to: a 50/50 blend with higher Sharpe and better stress-period returns than either alone
mechanism_chain.why: pairing captures underreaction more fully and covers a wider range of bear markets

design_rationale.reason_given: similar to Brooks (2017); avoids seasonality; lower turnover and trading costs than faster variants

design_rationale.choice: Theme-asset class signs fixed ex ante (asserted from theory, checked contemporaneously), never fitted for prediction
design_rationale.reason_given: persistent-impact premise implies equal contemporaneous and predictive signs; reduces data mining
longest possible history and less data-mining risk; backtest is a proof of concept
design_rationale.alternatives: broader real-time indicator set (mentioned as future work)

design_rationale.choice: Directional (time-series) views only, dropping Brooks (2017) relative-value legs
design_rationale.reason_given: focus of this paper; directional views compare each asset only with its own history, which makes adding commodities warranted

design_rationale.choice: Commodities traded on consumption-weighted country signals
design_rationale.reason_given: signals apply to the consuming countries of each commodity

design_rationale.choice: Data substitutions in early years (realized GDP/CPI lagged one quarter before 1991, IBOR before 1992, equity-only risk aversion before Dec 1987, Moody's Baa spread before Dec 2001 then HY OAS)
design_rationale.reason_given: data availability; realized-change substitute equals forecast change under a random walk

design_rationale.choice: Risk aversion = equal mix of 12-month equity excess return and 12-month credit spread change
design_rationale.reason_given: about half of equity return variation is discount-rate news (Campbell 1991); option-based measures lack coverage and history
design_rationale.alternatives: option-implied risk aversion (rejected for data reasons)

design_rationale.choice: Equal risk at every level (positions, asset class-theme portfolios, composites), 3-year trailing covariance, 10% volatility target
Bond futures and short-rate futures treated as separate asset classes in the aggregate (25 portfolios) but combined at equal risk within fixed income
Price trend benchmark = equal mix of 1-, 3-, 12-month excess returns with the same universe and construction
50/50 equal-risk blend of economic and price trend
design_rationale.reason_given: shared mechanism but moderate correlation and different drawdown timing

design_rationale.choice: Short-rate futures traded in the 2nd-4th contracts from expiry

evidence_map.result: Aggregate economic trend: 13.3%/yr over cash, 12.2% vol, Sharpe 1.1, correlation about 0 to S&P 500 and US 10-year bonds, 1970-2022, gross
evidence_map.tests: step 2 (macro news trends predict returns) and foundation 1
evidence_map.rules_out: that the strategy is a disguised long stock or bond position
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) exposure to other known premia (carry, value, price momentum inside the trade and risk aversion themes); hindsight in sign map and universe; realized-data revisions before 1991; costs (gross of fees and trading costs)
evidence_map.strength: moderate - 53 years and 59 markets, but hypothetical, gross, no t-stats or cost estimate

evidence_map.result: Positive in every decade (Sharpe 0.4 in 2010s to 1.6 in 1980s) and after Brooks (2017): 2017-2022 Sharpe 0.7, 2020-2022 Sharpe 1.2
evidence_map.tests: persistence; that Brooks (2017) results were not in-sample overfit
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) the out-of-sample window is six years dominated by one inflation and tightening shock made of short stock and bond positions; design was extended (commodities) after seeing earlier results

evidence_map.result: Positive Sharpe in nearly every asset (USD AUD only slightly negative), every theme and every asset class; composites nearly uncorrelated (0.06-0.07)
evidence_map.tests: foundation 1 holds broadly in macro assets; step 4
evidence_map.rules_out: concentration in one market, theme or asset class
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) per-asset Sharpe ratios of 0.1-0.5 are individually weak; a common factor (e.g. global rates or dollar) could drive many assets
evidence_map.strength: moderate to strong - breadth across 59 markets

evidence_map.result: Economic trend gained in each of the five worst S&P 500 drawdowns (avg about +60% vs about -39%) and five worst US 10-year Treasury drawdowns (avg about +39% vs about -14%)
evidence_map.rules_out: that the strategy loses in the classic stock or bond crises of the sample
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) only five episodes each, chosen ex post; several overlap with inflation and tightening shocks (1973-74, 1979-81, 2022) where one macro driver explains both

evidence_map.result: Price-economic trend correlation about 0.3 per asset, 0.4 aggregate; 50/50 blend Sharpe 1.5 vs price trend 1.4 and economic trend 1.1
evidence_map.rules_out: that economic trend is redundant with price trend
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) a gain that any moderately correlated positive-Sharpe stream would give; in currencies and commodities the blend adds nothing over price trend

evidence_map.result: Price trend averaged about +8% in economic trend's five worst drawdowns; economic trend about -1% in price trend's; Tech Bubble 1999-2000 and Oct 1987 as illustrations
evidence_map.rules_out: that the two strategies fail at the same times in the worst episodes
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) episode selection; only some episodes match the authors' story

evidence_map.result: 50/50 blend best on average in the five worst equity drawdowns (+68% vs +59% econ, +54% price) and bond drawdowns (+52% vs +47% price, +39% econ)
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) small n; averages driven by a few large episodes

evidence_map.result: Contemporaneous signs said to be 'empirically verified'
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) that some signs are unstable over time or regime (e.g. stock-bond correlation sign changes)

regimes.condition: Prices disconnected from fundamentals for a prolonged period (bubbles, e.g. June 1999-Dec 2000)
regimes.effect: economic trend loses (bearish bond, equity and dollar signals while markets rose) while price trend can profit; recovers when prices re-couple to news

regimes.condition: Reversals or crashes preceded by an economic catalyst (e.g. Oct 1987)
regimes.effect: price trend loses almost by construction; economic trend can profit with opposite positions

regimes.condition: Drawdowns triggered by falling growth expectations or hawkish central banks (GFC, 2018, 2022)
regimes.effect: economic trend profits; price trend does best in persistent drawdowns

regimes.condition: An asset class trending strongly over a short period
regimes.effect: economic trend takes on a conditional correlation to it (2020-2022 profits from short equities and bonds)

regimes.condition: High macro volatility (2018 sell-off, pandemic, 2021-22 inflation and tightening)
regimes.effect: strong out-of-sample returns, exceptional in the 2022 stock-bond bear market
weakest decade (4.1% at 9.9% vol, Sharpe 0.4); no explanation given
signals rely on realized data substitutes and equity-only risk aversion, so early results test a cruder version

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Monetary policy signs: appendix says easing is bullish currencies and bearish fixed income, which conflicts with Exhibit 1 and economic logic (rising 2-year yield: currency +, bonds -).
Number of building blocks: 20 asset class-theme portfolios with fixed income combined (C05 text, footnote 9, appendix) vs 25 with bonds and short rates separate in the aggregate (footnote 10).
Contemporaneous sign verification is claimed but no test or statistic is shown; signs could be regime-dependent.
Pre-1991 substitute assumes GDP growth and CPI inflation are random walks; equivalence never checked against post-1991 forecast data.
Point-in-time handling unclear: realized data lagged one quarter but data revisions and vintages not discussed; forecast release timing not given.

Unspecified construction details: signal-to-position mapping (sign only or magnitude, any scaling or z-scoring), how the two risk aversion inputs are standardised before combining, export weights for the trade basket, country consumption weights for commodities, rebalancing frequency.
Results are gross of fees and trading costs; no turnover or cost estimate is given despite the low-turnover claim.
Inflation-commodity sign appears only in Exhibit 1, not in the appendix rationale.
Part of the 'fundamental' signal is itself a price signal (equity momentum in risk aversion; trade theme in currencies is close to FX price momentum), which blurs the separation from price trend.
Macro-asset underreaction evidence is thinner than single-stock evidence.
Backtest is not frozen (results may vary with run date; discounting factors may be applied to suspected anomalies).
Citation and data-list inconsistencies: Hurst-Ooi-Pedersen dated 2014 vs 2017, several cited works missing from references, aluminum and copper start dates missing.

relations.why: same underreaction mechanism, different inputs; correlation 0.3-0.4; different drawdown timing; blend beats both
economic trend is its directional-only part, extended to commodities and to 2017-2022
prior evidence of macro underreaction in equity indices, the equity leg of this strategy
documented underreaction of fixed income to monetary policy surprises, the monetary policy theme in bonds
the trade theme in currencies (depreciation bearish the currency) is very similar to price momentum
near-zero long-run correlation and gains in their worst drawdowns
price plus economic trend outperforms in a diverse variety of drawdown environments

reasoning_map.forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Observable inputs: 12-month changes in consensus real GDP and CPI forecasts, 12-month change in the export-weighted exchange rate, 12-month change in 2-year yields, and the equal mix of 12-month equity excess return and credit-spread change, per country (consumption-weighted for commodities), mapped by the Exhibit 1 signs. Through step 2 (underreaction) they are said to lead returns of equity index, bond, short-rate, currency and commodity futures over the following months (monthly rebalanced; the decay horizon of the edge is not measured). They would stop working if markets absorbed macro news faster (more capital in macro systematic strategies), if prices stay decoupled from fundamentals for long periods (bubbles), if the sign map breaks (e.g. a change in the stock-bond correlation regime or in central bank credibility changes how inflation news moves equities, bonds and currencies), or in low macro-volatility periods like the 2010s.
reader_inferences: (reader) Rebalancing is monthly; the paper reports monthly returns but never states the trading frequency.
(reader) Positions appear to be taken by direction of the theme change; whether signal magnitude scales positions is not stated.
(reader) The monetary policy sign text in the appendix is likely a wording slip; Exhibit 1 and economic logic should be trusted.

(reader) Equity momentum in the risk aversion theme and the trade theme in currencies make part of 'economic trend' a price-based signal, which may account for some of the correlation with price trend.
(reader) Drawdown evidence is based on five ex-post chosen episodes per asset and overlaps with inflation shocks, so it is suggestive, not conclusive.
(reader) The 2017-2022 out-of-sample result is concentrated in one inflation-and-tightening regime (short stocks and bonds 2020-2022).
(reader) Pre-1991 realized-data signals may contain revised data that was not known at the time, adding look-ahead not discussed in the paper.
(reader) Sign stability across regimes (e.g. positive vs negative stock-bond correlation eras) is an untested assumption of the fixed sign map.
(reader) Net-of-cost performance is unknown; the low-turnover claim is not quantified.

claims.quote: tendency for new information to have a persistent impact on asset prices by positioning in each market on the basis of trends in macroeconomic fundamentals
claims.claim: Economic trend profits because news about fundamentals has a persistent price impact, so positioning on trends in macro fundamentals earns the drift.

claims.quote: returns over a 50+ year sample, and performance is pervasive across both markets and measures
claims.claim: Authors report consistently attractive risk-adjusted returns over 50+ years, pervasive across markets and themes (measures).
claims.reported_result: 50+ year sample (Jan 1970-Dec 2022); headline numbers in Exhibit 2-4

claims.quote: It exhibits low correlation to traditional risk premia on average and tends to perform exceptionally well during drawdown periods for traditional asset classes
claims.claim: Economic trend has low average correlation to traditional risk premia and does well in drawdowns of equities and bonds.
claims.reported_result: Qualitative here; numbers in Exhibit 2 and Exhibits 5, 8, 9

claims.quote: the two strategies are highly complementary. Combining the two leads to improved risk-adjusted performance and more robust drawdown protection than price
claims.claim: Economic trend and price trend-following are close relatives (both exploit under-reaction) yet complementary; blending them improves Sharpe and drawdown protection versus price trend alone.
claims.reported_result: Total Sharpe 1.1 econ / 1.4 price / 1.5 blend (Exhibit 6)

claims.quote: Trend-following is based on time series momentum
claims.claim: Price trend-following is defined as time-series momentum: long assets with recent positive returns, short assets with recent negative returns.
claims.exact_rule: Long assets with positive trailing return, short assets with negative trailing return (time series momentum).

claims.quote: has been documented to generate consistent positive returns across a wide range of assets over more than 120 years
claims.claim: Price trend-following has earned consistent positive returns across many assets for more than 120 years.
claims.reported_result: Cites Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen (2012); Lemperiere et al. (2014); Hurst, Ooi and Pedersen (2017)

claims.quote: Its persistent profitability stems from the tendency of asset prices to systematically underreact to new information
claims.claim: Trend profitability comes from systematic under-reaction of prices to new information, so positioning on recent trends profits as prices gradually adjust.

claims.quote: See Moskowitz, Ooi, and Pedersen (2012), Lemperiere, Deremble, Seager, Potters, and Bouchaud (2014), and Hurst, Ooi, and Pedersen (2017).
claims.claim: Footnote 2 cites three papers (Moskowitz-Ooi-Pedersen 2012; Lemperiere et al. 2014; Hurst-Ooi-Pedersen 2017) as evidence that time series momentum works across assets over very long samples.

claims.quote: Possible explanations of market reactions include herding and extrapolation of recent market movements.
claims.claim: Footnote 3 lists behavioural/theory papers on under-reaction (Barberis-Shleifer-Vishny 1998; Daniel-Hirshleifer-Subrahmanyam 1998; Hong-Stein 1999; Frazzini 2006) and offers herding and extrapolation of recent moves as possible explanations.

claims.quote: Many studies focus on underreaction in single-name equities
claims.claim: Footnote 4 notes under-reaction evidence is mostly in single stocks (Chan-Jegadeesh-Lakonishok 1996; Chan 2003; Frazzini 2006; Sinha 2016), with fewer macro-asset studies: Bhojraj and Swaminathan (2006) for international equity indices and Brooks, Katz and Lustig (2018) showing persistent bond-market under-reaction to monetary policy surprises.

claims.quote: investing on the basis of trends in fundamentals directly, as opposed to using price trends as a proxy for new information
claims.claim: Because prices under-react to news, one can trade trends in fundamentals directly instead of price trends as a proxy for news.

claims.quote: describes a broad approach to fundamental trend investing, called “macro momentum,” and presents evidence of its efficacy from 1970 through 2016
claims.claim: Brooks (2017) 'macro momentum' is the precursor strategy and showed efficacy 1970-2016; the current paper extends it to 2017-2022 out of sample.
claims.reported_result: Original evidence 1970-2016 (Brooks 2017)

claims.quote: we extend the original strategy described in Brooks (2017) and focus solely on its directional implementation
claims.claim: The economic trend strategy is the directional (outright long/short, no relative-value cross-section) version of Brooks (2017) macro momentum.
claims.exact_rule: Each asset is positioned long or short on its own signal sign; no cross-sectional ranking.

claims.quote: Returns are a convenient indicator. They’re continuous, readily available, and require little by way of modeling beyond specifying a horizon.
claims.claim: Price trend uses returns because they are continuous, available and need only a horizon, but returns are only an indirect proxy for fundamental news.

claims.quote: indirect reflection of fundamental news—one that can at times be misleading
claims.claim: Returns are an indirect and sometimes misleading reflection of fundamental news, which is why economic trend models news directly.

claims.quote: identifying the relevant fundamental variables that drive each asset’s price (e.g., inflation expectations impact bond prices)
claims.claim: First requirement of real-time economic trend: identify the fundamental variables that drive each asset's price (e.g. inflation expectations for bonds).
claims.exact_rule: Step 1: choose fundamental state variables per asset (here: growth, inflation, trade, monetary policy, risk aversion).

claims.quote: modeling trends in these fundamental variables in real-time (e.g., measuring real-time trends in inflation expectations for each market)
claims.claim: Second requirement: measure the trend in each fundamental variable in real time for each market.
claims.exact_rule: Step 2: compute a trailing trend (12-month change) of each state variable per market, using information available at the time.

claims.quote: a structural mapping from fundamental trends to asset prices (e.g., increasing inflation expectations in a country is bad news for its stock and bond markets, good news for its currency, etc.)
claims.claim: Third requirement: a sign mapping from each fundamental trend to each asset class (e.g. rising inflation expectations bearish stocks and bonds, bullish currency).
claims.exact_rule: Step 3: fixed theme x asset-class sign matrix (Exhibit 1).

claims.quote: Unlike price trend, economic trend will not invest where price action isn’t supported by underlying fundamental news.
claims.claim: Economic trend takes no position where price moves are not backed by fundamental news, unlike price trend.
claims.conditions: Differs from price trend: position follows fundamentals, not prices

claims.quote: The strategy will suffer when returns are disconnected from changes in fundamentals (as can happen) but will generate profits when asset prices begin to cue off fundamental news again.
claims.claim: Economic trend loses when prices decouple from fundamentals and profits again when prices respond to fundamental news.
claims.conditions: Fails when returns are disconnected from fundamentals (e.g. Tech Bubble, see Exhibit 7)

claims.quote: uses a similar set of signals to capture macroeconomic state variables as Brooks (2017) but extends the strategy to incorporate a broad set of commodity markets
claims.claim: The stylized strategy reuses the Brooks (2017) macro signals but adds commodities to the universe and tests 2017-2022 out of sample.
claims.exact_rule: Universe = equities, bonds, short rates, currencies, commodities; signals as Brooks (2017).

claims.quote: the equity market sell-off of 2018, the global pandemic, and the subsequent emergence of global inflation and associated monetary policy response
claims.claim: The 2017-2022 out-of-sample window is described as macro-volatile: 2018 equity sell-off, pandemic, then global inflation and policy tightening.
claims.reported_result: Out-of-sample window Jan 2017-Dec 2022
claims.conditions: Out-of-sample relative to Brooks (2017), but signal design was set in advance only loosely (same signals)

claims.quote: adjusted returns across asset classes from 1970 to 2022, with low correlation to traditional markets and strong performance during equity and bond market drawdowns
claims.claim: Authors summarise attractive risk-adjusted returns 1970-2022, low correlation to traditional markets, strong drawdown performance.
claims.reported_result: See Exhibit 2 (Sharpe 1.1 full sample) and Exhibits 5, 8, 9

claims.quote: sample period from 2017 onward and delivered exceptional returns during the stock and bond bear market of 2022
claims.claim: Economic trend kept performing in the out-of-sample period 2017 onward and earned exceptional returns in the 2022 stock and bond bear market.
claims.reported_result: Jan 2017-Dec 2022: 8.4% excess return, Sharpe 0.7 (Exhibit 2); Jan 2022-Sep 2022 equity drawdown window about +49% (Exhibit 5, chart read)

claims.quote: Because they share a common mechanism, economic trend and price trend tend to be positively, though modestly, correlated.
claims.claim: Shared under-reaction mechanism makes economic and price trend positively but modestly correlated.
claims.reported_result: Correlation about 0.3 asset level, 0.4 aggregate (C08)

claims.quote: strategy that combines price and economic trends thus outperforms either approach standalone
claims.claim: A combined price plus economic trend strategy has better risk-adjusted results than either alone (note: Exhibit 6 shows blend does not beat price trend in currencies or commodities).
claims.reported_result: Total Sharpe 1.5 blend vs 1.4 price, 1.1 econ (Exhibit 6)

claims.quote: Price trend tends to perform well in drawdowns that are persistent. Economic trend tends to perform well in drawdowns that have economic catalysts.
claims.claim: Price trend wins in persistent drawdowns, economic trend in drawdowns with an identifiable economic catalyst, so the two cover different stress scenarios.
claims.conditions: Persistent decline -> price trend; economic catalyst -> economic trend

claims.quote: Brooks (2017) excludes commodities in part because relative-value view construction in commodities is less intuitive
claims.claim: Commodities were excluded from Brooks (2017) because cross-sectional relative-value views are less intuitive; the directional design makes adding them reasonable.

claims.quote: we believe adding commodities to the universe is warranted.
claims.claim: Directional views compare an asset's mapped economic change only to its own time series, so commodities can be included.
claims.exact_rule: Commodity signals use consumption-weighted country signals; time-series (own-history) comparison only.

claims.quote: Our economic trend backtest uses simple 12-month trailing indicators, similar to Brooks (2017)
claims.claim: All five economic-trend signals are simple 12-month trailing changes.
claims.exact_rule: Signal_t = value_t minus value_(t-12 months) for each theme variable; sign mapped per Exhibit 1.

claims.quote: For both growth and inflation, we use 12-month changes in GDP growth forecasts and CPI inflation forecasts.
claims.claim: Growth signal = 12-month change in GDP growth forecast; inflation signal = 12-month change in CPI inflation forecast.
claims.exact_rule: growth_signal = GDPforecast_t - GDPforecast_(t-12m); inflation_signal = CPIforecast_t - CPIforecast_(t-12m); country-level.
claims.data_needed: Consensus Economics GDP and CPI forecasts (from 1991); OECD GDP and CPI realised (before)

claims.quote: we use 12-month changes in the local spot FX rate against an export-weighted basket.
claims.claim: International trade signal = 12-month change in local currency vs export-weighted basket (depreciation = positive trade-competitiveness signal for equities).
claims.exact_rule: trade_signal = -(12m % change in local currency vs export-weighted basket) i.e. depreciation positive; mapped by Exhibit 1.

claims.quote: We measure monetary policy trends using 12-month changes in short term bond yields.
claims.claim: Monetary policy signal = 12-month change in 2-year bond yield (IBOR before 1992).
claims.exact_rule: mp_signal = y2_t - y2_(t-12m); rising yield = tightening trend.

claims.quote: And we measure risk aversion trends using an equal weighted combination of 12-month trailing equity market returns and 12-month changes in credit spreads.
claims.claim: Risk aversion signal = equal-weighted combination of 12-month equity return and (negative) 12-month change in credit spreads.
claims.exact_rule: risk_signal = 0.5*z(12m equity excess return) + 0.5*z(-12m change in credit spread); equity-only before Dec 1987 (standardisation of the two legs is not specified).
claims.data_needed: Equity index returns (DataStream); Moody's Baa-10Y CMT spread to 2001; Bloomberg Global High Yield index after

claims.quote: Exhibit 1: Summary of Economic Trend Signals
claims.claim: Sign matrix: rising growth forecast is + for equities, - bonds, + currencies, + commodities; rising inflation forecast - equities, - bonds, + currencies, + commodities; export-weighted FX depreciation + equities, - bonds, - currencies, - commodities; rising 2y yield - equities, - bonds, + currencies, - commodities; strong equity return/narrowing spreads + equities, - bonds, + currencies, + commodities.
claims.exact_rule: Position sign = (signal change direction) x matrix sign. Growth(E+,FI-,FX+,Cmd+); Inflation(E-,FI-,FX+,Cmd+); Trade(E+,FI-,FX-,Cmd-); Monetary(E-,FI-,FX+,Cmd-); RiskAversion(E+,FI-,FX+,Cmd+). Commodities use consumption-weighted signals over consuming countries.

claims.quote: The signs of these relationships are based on theoretically motivated and empirically verified “other things equal” contemporaneous relationships between returns and news about each theme.
claims.claim: Signs are fixed in advance from theory and verified contemporaneous return/news relationships, not fit to predictive performance.

claims.quote: Economic trend is built on the premise that news tends to have a persistent impact on asset prices, which implies that contemporaneous and predictive relationships between returns and news must have the same sign.
claims.claim: If news has persistent price impact, the contemporaneous sign of news on returns equals the predictive sign, so contemporaneous relationships can fix the sign of the signals.

claims.quote: This restriction reduces the scope for data mining in a real-world setting: to trade on economic trends, you must demonstrate that news about the state variable has a contemporaneous impact on returns of the same sign.
claims.claim: The same-sign restriction limits data mining: a state variable is only tradable if its news has a same-sign contemporaneous return impact.
claims.exact_rule: Admit a state variable only if the contemporaneous return response to its change has the sign used for prediction.

claims.quote: performance is associated with declining inflation, expansionary monetary policy trends, improving trade competitiveness, and declining risk aversion
claims.claim: Examples of the contemporaneous mapping: strong equity performance goes with declining inflation, easier policy, better trade competitiveness and lower risk aversion; growth increases are good for equities.

claims.quote: Therefore, in this period we use 12-month changes in GDP growth and CPI inflation instead.
claims.claim: Before 1991 (forecasts unavailable for many countries) realised 12-month changes in GDP growth and CPI inflation replace forecast changes; 12-month changes avoid seasonality and imply lower turnover and costs than faster variants.
claims.exact_rule: 1970-1990: growth/inflation signal = 12m change in YoY real GDP growth / YoY CPI (lagged one quarter, see C14). From 1991: 12m change in consensus forecast.
claims.conditions: Data substitution by period

claims.quote: From 1970 through 1991 we use changes in IBOR rates instead of two-year bond yields. This is due to data availability.
claims.claim: Monetary-policy signal uses changes in IBOR rates through 1991 and 2-year yields afterwards.
claims.exact_rule: 1970-1991: 12m change in IBOR rates; 1992 on: 12m change in 2-year government yield.

claims.quote: From 1970 through November 1987 risk aversion is represented entirely by 12-month equity market momentum.
claims.claim: Risk aversion is equity momentum only until Nov 1987, then equal weight of equity momentum and credit-spread change; credit proxy is Moody's Baa minus 10Y CMT before Dec 2001, then Bloomberg Global High Yield Corporate index.
claims.exact_rule: Jan 1970-Nov 1987: risk = 12m equity return. Dec 1987-Nov 2001: 50% 12m equity return + 50% 12m change in (Baa yield - 10Y CMT). From Dec 2001: spread leg = Bloomberg Global High Yield Corporate index (unhedged).
claims.data_needed: Moody's Seasoned Baa yield, 10Y CMT, Bloomberg Global High Yield Corporate index
claims.conditions: Data substitution by period

claims.quote: It is possible to extract more theoretically appealing measures of risk aversion using asset prices (e.g. options) but there is insufficient asset coverage and history to utilize this data here.

claims.quote: Campbell (1991) shows that approximately 50% of the variation in equity returns is driven by discount rates which motivates the inclusion of equity market momentum within the risk aversion theme.
claims.claim: Campbell (1991): about half of equity return variation reflects discount-rate changes, motivating equity momentum as a risk-aversion proxy.

claims.quote: in commodities we use consumption-weighted signals across all themes (i.e., the signals apply to consuming countries of that commodity).
claims.claim: Commodity positions use consumption-weighted country signals (weights are consuming countries of that commodity).
claims.exact_rule: Commodity signal_t = sum_over_consumer_countries(w_c * theme_signal_c,t), w_c = consumption share; then sign per Exhibit 1.

claims.quote: Our asset universe includes 15 global equity futures, 9 bond futures, 7 interest rate futures, 8 currency forwards, and 20 commodity futures.
claims.claim: Universe: 15 equity index futures, 9 bond futures, 7 short-rate futures, 8 currency forwards, 20 commodity futures (59 markets).
claims.exact_rule: Universe lists in C15 and Exhibit 3.
claims.data_needed: Futures/forward return series (Bloomberg, Citi, Reuters, IFS, DataStream)

claims.quote: For each of the five economic themes we create a portfolio for each of the four asset classes, leaving us with 20 asset class-theme portfolios
claims.claim: Build one portfolio per theme x asset class (5 x 4 = 20).
claims.exact_rule: Within each theme-asset class portfolio: each asset gets a view from the theme signal, equal risk to each view, scaled to constant vol using 3-year trailing covariance.

claims.quote: These asset class-theme portfolios allocate equal risk to individual asset views (within an asset class) and are scaled to constant volatility at each point in time using a 3-year trailing covariance matrix.
claims.claim: Within an asset-class/theme portfolio each asset view gets equal risk and the portfolio is scaled to constant vol with a trailing 3-year covariance matrix; bond and rate futures are combined into fixed-income theme portfolios.
claims.exact_rule: Weights proportional to sign / sigma_i with portfolio vol target from trailing 36-month covariance; target level 10% (see composites).

claims.quote: We aggregate these asset class-theme portfolios into equal risk-weighted composite portfolios.
claims.claim: Three composites: asset class composite (all themes equal risk within one asset class), theme composite (one theme across asset classes) and aggregate composite (equal risk across all asset class-theme portfolios).
claims.exact_rule: Aggregate = equal risk-weighted across asset class-theme portfolios; rescaled to 10% vol.

claims.quote: for the purposes of the aggregate portfolios, we treat bond futures and short-term interest rate futures as separate asset classes (i.e., the economic trend-following composite uses 25 asset class-theme portfolios).
claims.claim: In the aggregate, bonds and short rates count as separate asset classes, so the composite combines 25 (5 themes x 5 asset classes) portfolios; the 'fixed income' bars combine the two at equal risk.
claims.exact_rule: Aggregate = equal risk over 5 themes x {equity, bond, short rate, FX, commodity}.

claims.quote: weighted combination of 1-month, 3-month, and 12-month trailing asset returns as factors
claims.claim: Price trend benchmark: equal-weighted 1m, 3m and 12m trailing excess returns as signals; same universe and construction as economic trend.
claims.exact_rule: Price signal = equal-weight combination of sign (or scaled value) of 1m, 3m and 12m trailing excess return, per Hurst-Ooi-Pedersen (2017).

claims.quote: target 10% constant volatility at each point in time using a trailing 3-year covariance matrix.
claims.claim: All composites (economic and price trend) are scaled to 10% annual volatility using a trailing 3-year covariance matrix.
claims.exact_rule: Scale composite so predicted annual vol = 10% using covariance estimated on trailing 36 months, updated each month.

claims.quote: Using only 12-month trailing asset returns would give directionally similar results as shown below.

claims.quote: Prior to 1991, we use one-year changes in realized year-on-year real GDP growth, lagged one quarter
claims.claim: Growth signal: Consensus Economics forecast changes from 1991; before 1991 one-year change in realised YoY real GDP growth lagged one quarter (OECD), equivalent to a random-walk forecast. Rationale for signs: growth up is bullish equities (cash flow), commodities (demand), currencies (Balassa-Samuelson) and bearish bonds (inflation pressure and higher real rates).
claims.exact_rule: Growth_t: >=1991 12m change in Consensus real GDP growth forecast; <1991 12m change in YoY real GDP growth, lagged 1 quarter.

claims.quote: Prior to 1991, we use one-year changes in realized year-on-year CPI inflation, lagged one quarter
claims.claim: Inflation signal: Consensus CPI forecast changes from 1991; before 1991 one-year change in realised YoY CPI lagged one quarter (OECD). Signs: rising inflation bearish equities (Katz and Lustig 2017), bullish currencies (Clarida and Waldman 2008), bearish fixed income.
claims.exact_rule: Inflation_t: >=1991 12m change in Consensus CPI forecast; <1991 12m change in YoY CPI, lagged 1 quarter.
claims.conditions: Disclosure text omits the commodity sign, Exhibit 1 shows +

claims.quote: A depreciating currency is bullish for equities (exports become more competitive), bearish for currencies (very similar to price momentum), bearish for fixed income
claims.claim: International trade signal rationale: depreciation helps equity exports, is bearish for the currency itself (like price momentum), bearish for bonds (less pressure to cut rates) and bearish for commodities (more expensive in local currency of consumers).
claims.data_needed: DataStream spot exchange rates vs export-weighted basket

claims.quote: From 1992 onwards, we use two-year yields, while prior to 1992 we use Libor and its international equivalents.

claims.exact_rule: Monetary_t = 12m change in 2y yield (>=1992) or Libor-equivalent (<1992); signs per Exhibit 1 (E-, FI-, FX+, Cmd-).
claims.conditions: Cited support: Bernanke and Kuttner (2005) equities; Eichenbaum and Evans (1995) currencies

claims.quote: The second is one-year changes in credit spreads. Changes in credit spreads are computed using Moody’s Corporate Yields relative to U.S. treasuries until 2001 and then Bloomberg Global High Yield Corporate OAS.
claims.claim: Risk aversion: equal weight of one-year equity excess return (DataStream) and one-year change in credit spreads (Moody's corporate yield vs Treasuries until 2001, then Bloomberg Global High Yield OAS); rising risk sentiment is bullish equities, commodities and currencies and bearish bonds.
claims.exact_rule: Risk_t = 0.5*12m equity excess return + 0.5*(-12m change in spread); spread = Moody's Baa-Treasury to 2001, Bloomberg Global HY OAS after.
claims.data_needed: DataStream equity returns; Moody's yields; Bloomberg Global High Yield OAS
claims.conditions: Footnote 8 calls the post-2001 series the 'Stats Index Unhedged', disclosures say OAS
